tabs.title: Understanding
tabs.description: Understand the central ideas and the people.

tabs.title: Using What You Read
tabs.description: Apply the idea in a new situation.

questions.q: What was the problem with the students' first idea of putting up a sign by the stream?
choices: It was planned for the wrong side of their school.
The engineer said signs were never allowed near streams.
It did not address rubbish entering the water through street drains.
The town did not have enough volunteers to paint it.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Why can wrappers left on the pavement end up in a stream?
choices: A cleaner puts them directly into the river.
Rainwater carries them into a drain and pipe.
Wind always pushes them uphill from the bus stop.
They travel along the street because buses create vibrations.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Why did the students divide the street into sections before counting litter?
choices: To stop people from using the bus stop during the project.
To give every volunteer exactly the same number of wrappers.
To find the fastest route between their school and the library.
To compare places and see where the problem was greatest.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: What does the difference between the bus stop and the library suggest?
choices: The busy bus-stop area needed more attention than the quieter part of the street.
The library was closed on both afternoons.
The library staff had already collected every wrapper.
The students had counted the same wrappers twice near the bus stop.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Why did changing the bin's collection time make sense?
choices: There was no rubbish near the stop in the mornings.
The café owner wanted the bin to be removed permanently.
The bin was full later in the day when many people were using the stop.
The bus driver was responsible for collecting all street rubbish.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Why did the students avoid saying that the problem had disappeared?
choices: Weather and rubbish from other streets could still cause trouble.
The engineer had forbidden them to publish a result.
Their first count had found no rubbish at all.
All the people who used the street had moved away.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: What was the purpose of inviting neighbours to share their own photos?
choices: The students wanted a competition for the best camera.
More observations could help reveal problems beyond the original street.
Only residents could legally discuss the stream.
The council had stopped cleaning drains entirely.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Your school finds wrappers near a playground. What should it do before choosing a solution?
choices: Put a warning sign at the first place anyone notices litter.
Blame the youngest pupils before collecting information.
Assume that all wrappers came from one shop.
Investigate where the rubbish comes from and how it travels.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: A stream looks cleaner after one month. What would be a sensible next step?
choices: Stop collecting any evidence because the project is over.
Keep checking during different weather conditions.
Remove every bin from the street.
Tell neighbours that no other changes are possible.
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.

questions.q: Which question would best continue the students' final lesson?
choices: Which volunteer picked up the most wrappers?
Can a sign beside the river make everybody feel better?
Who should be blamed for everything that happened last year?
Where does the problem begin, and which practical step could prevent it?
questions.explanation: The students' investigation connects rubbish to street drains, timetables, local observations and practical changes rather than blame.
